docs.text:
Contributors

PaperManager is open source and grows with other people's pull requests. Thank you to Antoine Luciano for researcher CVs, the duplicate-people finder and surname order on the People page (#36, People guide).

docs.title: Add a paper
docs.text: Drag in a PDF or paste an arXiv, DOI or PubMed link. The metadata is looked up for you; you check it and press save.

docs.title: PaperManager reads it
docs.text: In the background it writes a summary, pulls out figures, tables and references, and suggests topics and tags.

docs.title: You read, ask and connect
docs.text: Read the PDF with the summary, a guided tour and visual explanations beside it, then ask questions across everything you have read.

docs.title: One library for every paper
docs.text:
Search titles, authors, your notes and highlights and the full text in one box, ranked, with every hit showing why it matched. Narrow it by date added, year, reading status, rating, document type, project, tag, topic or venue, or by whether a paper has a PDF, a note or highlights; the whole view is in the URL. Continue reading and Recently added sit on the landing page.

Library · Search and filters

docs.title: A profile for every author
docs.text:
Each researcher gets a CV built from OpenAlex, ORCID, Wikidata and their homepage, checked against the papers in your library so a namesake is not mistaken for them. People listed under several spellings are found and merged in one click. Contributed by Antoine Luciano.

People

docs.title: Everything about a paper in one view
docs.text:
The left side switches between the PDF, the summary, figures, tables, references and related papers. The right side keeps your notes, highlights and a chat about the paper open beside it.

Reading a paper

docs.title: A guided tour through a long paper
docs.text:
An overview, what you can skip, and 6–12 stops that jump to the passages that matter, with the concepts each one relies on.

Concepts, tour and concept map

docs.title: How a whole project fits together
docs.text:
The key concepts of every paper in a project and how they relate, as a graph you can filter by author, year and kind of concept.

Concept map

docs.title: Ask your whole library
docs.text:
The knowledge chat answers from your papers and cites them; a citation opens the paper beside the chat. You see every lookup the model makes and a sources row under each answer. Answers can carry figure strips, concept cards (formulas, plots, animations) and 3D structures (PDB entries, ligands, alignments) you can rotate. Narrow a question with @project:, @topic: or @paper:, branch off from any question, stop or retry an answer, or let it search the web too.

Knowledge chat

docs.title: A long read from your own papers
docs.text:
Ask a question or pick a project and a report is written in the background: sections, citations that link to your papers, a reference list, export as HTML or Markdown. Every model call it makes shows up on the Tokens page with its cost; the chat can also propose improvements to the app, which everyone can vote on.

Reports · Tokens · Suggestions

docs.title: Who publishes what at NeurIPS, ICML, CVPR, ACL, ...
docs.text:
Browse the accepted papers of 22 conference series by institution (rank, research-area mix, collaborators, every paper) or by topic: type one or paste an abstract and see which universities and companies publish most on it and the closest papers, one click from your library. One search box covers all loaded conferences at once: papers, authors, and where a topic is published, per conference and over the years.

Conference explorer

docs.title: New preprints, and papers like this abstract
docs.text:
Switch on the optional paper feed and a digest of new arXiv, bioRxiv and medRxiv preprints is ranked for you by a small model trained on your own library; it runs on your server and nothing about you is sent out. Similar papers takes an abstract, even one for a paper that does not exist yet, and lists the closest papers of your library and the feed with a score.

Paper feed · Similar papers · Switching the embedding model

docs.title: See it in action
docs.text:
Three short films, each recorded from a real library:

  • Ask the library (41 s): the chat queries the graph, pulls in 16 figures, spins a 3D structure and links every source.
  • The five you need (40 s): one query and four filters take 1,173 papers down to five.
  • One paper, taken apart (36 s): the AlphaFold 3 paper is split into pages, figures, claims and authors, then tied to the papers that cite it.

More on the project page. Music in the first two: Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text:
graph LR
    UI["React app"] --> API["FastAPI backend"]
    MCP["Claude via MCP"] --> API
    API --> DB[("Neo4j<br/>knowledge graph")]
    API --> Drive["Google Drive<br/>PDFs and figures"]
    API --> LLM["Claude / any<br/>OpenAI-compatible model"]
    API --> Ext["Semantic Scholar<br/>CrossRef · arXiv"]

Every paper, author, topic, project, note and concept is a node in one Neo4j graph, so the same data powers the library, the chat, the reports, the concept map and the Graph page's Cypher query panel. PDFs stay in your own Google Drive. More in Architecture.

PaperManager is open source. The project page at niklas-abraham.de has the story behind it; issues and pull requests are welcome on GitHub.

docs.title: Set up with your coding agent
docs.text:
The quickest way to your own PaperManager is to let a coding agent install it. This works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other agents that can run commands on your computer. Open one in any folder and say:

Set up PaperManager for me by following https://github.com/NiklasAbraham/PaperManager/blob/main/DEPLOY.md

DEPLOY.md is a runbook written for the agent. It tells the agent to:

  1. Check your machine. Git and Docker must be present and Docker must be running. If something is missing, the agent explains how to install it and asks before installing.
  2. Ask you a few questions, one at a time:
    • your login name
    • which AI account you have: Anthropic, OpenAI, both, or your own OpenAI-compatible server
    • where to keep PDFs: on this computer (default) or in Google Drive
    • an accent colour for the app
  3. Write .env. The agent generates the database password and session secret itself. You paste your API key into the file yourself, so it never passes through the chat.
  4. Build and start the app with Docker. The first build takes about 10 minutes.
  5. Hand you one command to set your password in your own terminal.
  6. Run scripts/check_setup.py. It checks the database, the AI provider (with one tiny test message) and the file storage, then shows the address to open.

docs.title: What your answers change
docs.text:
Every answer is stored in .env, and the app reads it at startup:

Answer Setting Effect Anthropic key ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Summaries, topics, claims and the concept map run on Claude Haiku 4.5. Chat and concept visualisations use Claude Sonnet/Opus OpenAI key OPENAI_API_KEY Summaries and chat run on GPT-5 mini Own server LITELLM_ENDPOINT, LITELLM_MODEL Any OpenAI-compatible API (LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Ollama, vLLM) runs the fast tasks PDFs on this computer STORAGE_BACKEND=local Files go into the Docker volume paper_files. No Google account needed PDFs in Drive STORAGE_BACKEND=drive Files go to a Google Drive folder (setup) Accent colour UI_ACCENT Buttons, links and highlights use your colour (a preset name or any #RRGGBB)

AI_PROVIDER=auto uses the first configured provider in this order: your own server, then Anthropic, then OpenAI. Set AI_PROVIDER or FAST_MODEL to override that choice. If your own server fails and an Anthropic key is set, the fast tasks retry on Claude Haiku (AI_FALLBACK=false turns that off). The model menus in the app show the active model by name, and Claude options appear only for users who have a Claude key.

Two optional features stay off or at their defaults unless you ask for them: the paper feed (PAPER_FEED=true) and another embedding model (EMBED_MODEL). Their data (/app/data/feed, /app/data/vectors) sits on the same paper_files volume as your PDFs.

To change something later, edit .env and run docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml up -d. A colour or model change needs no rebuild.

docs.title: Without an agent
docs.text: Every step in DEPLOY.md is a plain shell command, so you can follow it yourself. The hosting guide covers Heroku, servers and Google Drive in detail.

docs.title: DB: Neo4j Aura (cloud) over SQLite
docs.text: Papers, people, topics, and tags are naturally a graph. Enables path queries, co-authorship derivation, topic clustering. Free tier (200k nodes / 400k relationships) sufficient for personal use.

docs.title: Tags as nodes, not property arrays
docs.text: Tags are first-class citizens for filtering and browsing. (Paper)-[:TAGGED]->(Tag) lets you query "all papers with this tag" efficiently.

docs.title: Topic ≠ Tag
docs.text:
• Topic = formal research area, linked to Person specialties
  • Tag = free-form personal label (source, status, context, anything)

docs.title: Notes as separate nodes
docs.text: Notes need their own @mention and #topic relationships. A text field on Paper would lose this graph power.

docs.title: INVOLVES relationship with role property
docs.text: Instead of many typed relationships for workflow states, one INVOLVES {role} relationship keeps the schema flexible. New roles can be invented freely without schema changes.

docs.title: Metadata extraction: four-layer chain
docs.text:
1. DOI regex → Semantic Scholar API (preferred) or CrossRef (fallback) — covers ~80–90% of papers
  2. Ollama + llama3.2:3b local LLM — for papers without DOI (drafts, internal reports)
  3. Regex heuristics — last resort, user corrects in UI
  4. Abstract fallback: ABSTRACT_RE regex → Claude Haiku

metadata_source field on Paper node records which layer was used. Semantic Scholar also returns topics + citation count → auto-populates Topic nodes.

docs.title: MCP server shares the same service layer as FastAPI
docs.text: db/queries/ and services/ are framework-neutral. FastAPI routers/ and MCP tools/ are two thin entry-point layers over the same logic. Every capability is available both via HTTP and via Claude Desktop tool calls. PDF upload is intentionally not exposed as an MCP tool — file upload via browser only.

docs.title: No Collection node (for now)
docs.text: Projects serve a similar purpose and are already in scope. Can revisit if the need for lightweight grouping (reading lists) emerges.

docs.title: Backend: FastAPI
docs.text: Python-native, strong async support, automatic OpenAPI docs.

docs.title: Frontend: React + Vite + Tailwind
docs.text: Standard modern SPA stack; fast HMR during development.

docs.title: Knowledge Chat: agentic tool-use over hybrid retrieval
docs.text: Instead of stuffing all paper text into context, the backend pre-loads a relevance-ranked subset and gives Claude two tools: run_cypher (live graph queries) and semantic_search (vector similarity). Claude decides what additional data it needs. This keeps context manageable while allowing Claude to chase any lead in the graph.

docs.title: Vector embeddings on Paper nodes
docs.text: 768-dim Ollama nomic-embed-text embeddings stored directly on Paper.embedding. A Neo4j vector index (paper_embeddings) enables ANN cosine search at query time. Chosen over a separate vector store (Pinecone, etc.) to keep the stack minimal.

docs.title: Hybrid retrieval: vector + recency fallback
docs.text: Vector search alone fails when embeddings haven't been generated yet (cold start). The recency fallback (10 most recently added papers) ensures Knowledge Chat is useful from day one without a backfill step.

docs.title: Conversation compaction with structured working memory
docs.text: Simple truncation loses context. Claude Haiku extracts a JSON block of key findings, open questions, and decisions before compaction. Specific numbers and paper titles survive in the structured JSON even after the messages are replaced.

docs.title: Claims as graph nodes
docs.text: Claim extraction enables evidence-level queries via Cypher. Claims are NOT injected into Knowledge Chat context by default (would bloat it); Claude pulls them on demand via run_cypher when it needs evidence-level detail.

docs.title: Chapters for books and lecture decks
docs.text: document_type on Paper controls the upload pipeline. Books and lecture decks skip summary/figures/references/claims but support chapters. Chapters are detected in three passes: Docling structural → regex → Ollama AI.

docs.title: Blogs as first-class nodes
docs.text: Technical blog posts (Distill, Lil'Log, etc.) are valuable context alongside papers. Blog (feed) and BlogPost (individual post) nodes allow the same tag/project/chat workflows used for papers to apply to blog content.

docs.title: Annotations (PDF highlights) stored in Neo4j
docs.text: Highlights stored as Annotation nodes linked to Paper, not as PDF metadata. This keeps annotations queryable and database-portable.

docs.title: Author tracking with Semantic Scholar
docs.text: Person.tracked = true + Person.s2_author_id enables automatic import of new papers. S2 is queried periodically; new papers are ingested just like URL ingest.

docs.title: JWT authentication with admin-managed users
docs.text: Single-user primary focus, but multi-user support needed for collaboration. JWT stored in localStorage; admin user manages create/update/delete. Admin capabilities restricted to username niklas in current implementation.

docs.title: Rate limiting as in-process middleware
docs.text: Sliding-window rate limiter in services/rate_limit.py (no Redis dependency). Stricter limits on /auth/login to prevent brute-force attacks.

docs.title: Docker Compose + Traefik for production
docs.text: Three services: Neo4j, FastAPI backend, Nginx-served React frontend. Traefik handles SSL (Let's Encrypt) and routing. Neo4j and backend are internal-only; only the Nginx container is internet-facing.

docs.title: Conference data on disk, not in Neo4j
docs.text: A conference is 3,000–9,000 papers and as many people; as Paper and Person nodes they would swamp the library, the duplicate scanner and the free-tier node limit. Each conference-year is a JSON file plus a float16 embedding matrix under /data/conferences; only "+ Library" writes to the graph.

docs.title: Official miniconf feeds first, Paper Copilot for the rest
docs.text: NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, CVPR, ICCV and ECCV publish every accepted paper with each author's institution as one JSON file, so no scraping and no OpenReview profile crawl (OpenReview's API refuses anonymous clients). Paper Copilot's lists cover the other venues and older years.

docs.title: bge-small on CPU through transformers, no new dependency
docs.text: transformers and torch are already installed for Docling. bge-small-en-v1.5 (33 M parameters) embeds a 6,500-paper conference in two minutes from titles, or 3,000–6,000 papers with abstracts in 7–15 minutes, on four CPU threads, in the background, and needs no API key, so the feature works in the default self-hosted setup.

docs.title: One area taxonomy for every conference, assigned zero-shot
docs.text: 24 hand-described areas instead of per-conference clustering: the same area has the same name and colour at every venue, so conferences can be compared. Embeddings are centred on the conference mean before assignment; without it the most generic area absorbed a fifth of NeurIPS.

docs.title: One ranked search over every source, scored in Python
docs.text: The old /search passed the raw query to two Lucene indexes (titles/abstracts/summaries and notes), crashed on : or -, and could not find a paper by author, DOI, highlight or full text. Now each source (paper fields, author/topic/tag names, venue, notes, highlights, claims, full text, DOI/arXiv id) gets its own Lucene query, and the per-paper merge, coverage check and scoring happen in Python (services/library_search/). Lucene scores are not comparable across indexes, so each source is normalised by its best score and weighted; title and author bonuses come from the title and names themselves. Pure functions, so the ranking is unit-tested without Neo4j, and the MCP library_search tool uses the same engine.

docs.title: Every word must match somewhere, relaxed only when nothing does
docs.text: Lucene's default OR returned any paper with any word ("antibody docking" → every antibody paper). A hit must now cover every query word across its fields (author + title counts); only when no paper does are partial matches shown, flagged relaxed.

docs.title: standard-folding analyzer, indexes rebuilt at startup
docs.text: Case and accents must not matter (Kynkaanniemi = Kynkäänniemi). The search indexes moved to Neo4j's standard-folding analyzer and the query terms are folded the same way in Python (prefix and fuzzy terms bypass Lucene's analyzer). db/schema.py drops and rebuilds an index whose analyzer differs: seconds on this library, and simpler than versioned index names.

docs.title: Full text in Lucene, not CONTAINS
docs.text: The MCP tool scanned toLower(p.raw_text) CONTAINS over every paper: 220–270 ms per query on 36 MB of text. A full-text index on raw_text (eventually consistent, so uploads do not wait) costs 13 MB and answers in single-digit milliseconds.

docs.title: Hybrid by reciprocal-rank fusion, semantic weight scaled by confidence
docs.text: Library embeddings reuse the conference explorer's bge-small (no new dependency), stored in a file like the conference vectors, synced incrementally by a background thread. Semantic and lexical lists are fused by weighted RRF; the semantic weight shrinks when even the best cosine is low (jargon the model does not know), the lexical weight when the query is a long question.

docs.title: Library citations as a prior
docs.text: Among many papers matching "flow matching", the one most cited by the library's own papers is almost always the one meant. Scores are multiplied by 1 + 0.12 ln(1 + citing papers).

docs.title: Hosting your own PaperManager
docs.text:
Easiest: let your coding agent do it

Tell Claude Code, Codex or another coding agent: "Set up PaperManager for me by following https://github.com/NiklasAbraham/PaperManager/blob/main/DEPLOY.md". It asks a few questions and runs the local setup below for you. See Set up with your agent.

This guide sets up your own instance with your own database and your own keys. You can run it on your own computer (localhost) or on Heroku. Both use the same container image, Dockerfile.selfhost. It holds the React frontend, served by nginx, and the FastAPI backend, and serves both from one port. The login cookie only works when the page and the API come from the same origin, so they share that port.

docker-compose.example.yml mirrors the maintainer's production stack (Traefik, his domain, a remote GPU machine). Don't use it. Use docker-compose.selfhost.yml or heroku.yml.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Thing Required? Used for Git and Docker (Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows) yes building and running the app An Anthropic API key (console.anthropic.com) or an OpenAI API key (platform.openai.com) one of them summaries, topics, chat. With Anthropic the fast tasks run on Claude Haiku 4.5; with OpenAI everything runs on GPT-5 mini A Google account plus a Google Cloud project only for Drive storage, and always on Heroku PDFs in Google Drive. Locally, STORAGE_BACKEND=local keeps them in a Docker volume An OpenAI-compatible endpoint (LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Ollama) optional runs the fast tasks on your own model A Heroku account plus the Heroku CLI only for Heroku hosting A Neo4j AuraDB Free instance (console.neo4j.io) only for Heroku the database (locally, Docker runs Neo4j for you)

Expect around 2 GB of RAM for the app container. The PDF layout model (Docling) runs inside it and loads PyTorch.

docs.title: Step 1: get the code and create .env
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/NiklasAbraham/PaperManager.git
cd PaperManager
cp .env.example .env

Edit .env. Keep it private, since it is your secrets file and is git-ignored. Change these values and leave everything else at its default:

NEO4J_PASSWORD=<any long random string>        # locally: Docker creates the DB with this password
JWT_SECRET_KEY=<output of: openssl rand -hex 32>
DEFAULT_USER_NAME=<your login name>             # the owner/admin account
DEFAULT_USER_PASSWORD=                          # leave empty; you set it in step 4
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...                    # or OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
STORAGE_BACKEND=local                           # or drive, with GOOGLE_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID from step 2
UI_ACCENT=violet                                # or blue, teal, green, amber, rose, slate, #RRGGBB

# The maintainer's private infrastructure: switch it off
DOCLING_MODE=local
INFERENCE_MANAGER_URL=
HERMIONE_HOST=
LITELLM_ENDPOINT=
LITELLM_EMBED_MODEL=

Keep comments on their own line in the real file: Docker reads KEY= # note as the value # note. The comments above are only there to explain each line.

For your own model on the fast tasks, point LiteLLM at any OpenAI-compatible API, for example LITELLM_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, LITELLM_API_KEY=<openrouter key>, LITELLM_MODEL=google/gemma-3-27b-it.

Leave CLAUDE_CODE_USERS and CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN empty. That feature runs chats on the server owner's personal Claude subscription, and only the owner may use it. If you have your own Claude Pro/Max plan and want it for yourself, set CLAUDE_CODE_USERS=<your login name>. Then put the output of claude setup-token (from Claude Code) into CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. Never list other people there.

docs.title: Step 2: Google Drive access (once, on your own computer)
docs.text:
Skip this step locally with STORAGE_BACKEND=local. On Heroku it is required, because Heroku has no disk to keep files on. For Drive locally, also uncomment the two credentials.json / token.json lines in docker-compose.selfhost.yml.

  1. Go to console.cloud.google.com and create a project. Open APIs & Services → Library, then enable the Google Drive API.
  2. Open APIs & Services → OAuth consent screen. Choose user type External, fill in the app name and your e-mail, and add yourself as a test user.
  3. Open APIs & Services → Credentials → Create credentials → OAuth client ID, with application type Desktop app. Download the JSON and save it as backend/credentials.json.
  4. In Google Drive, create a folder for the PDFs. Its ID is the last part of the folder URL (https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/<THIS>). Put it into GOOGLE_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID.
  5. Create the login token. A browser window opens; log in and allow access:
python3 -m venv .venv-drive
.venv-drive/bin/pip install google-auth-oauthlib google-api-python-client
.venv-drive/bin/python backend/scripts/setup_drive_oauth.py

This writes backend/token.json. Both credentials.json and token.json are git-ignored. Never commit them.

docs.title: Step 3a: run on localhost
docs.text:
docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml up -d --build   # first build takes ~10 min
docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml logs -f app      # wait for "Application startup complete"

Create your account (step 4), then open http://localhost:8080.

  • Stop: docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml down. Your data stays in the neo4j_data volume (the graph) and the paper_files volume (PDFs, figures, conference datasets, and under /app/data the embedding vectors in vectors/ and, with the paper feed on, feed/). down -v deletes both.
  • Update: git pull, then run the up -d --build command again.

docs.title: Optional: paper feed and embedding model
docs.text:
Both are off or default unless you set them in .env (then up -d again):

  • PAPER_FEED=true switches on the paper feed, a digest of new preprints ranked by your library. Its database lives in PAPER_FEED_DIR.
  • EMBED_MODEL chooses the model behind library search, the feed and similar papers. The default BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 needs nothing more; for another one, and for doing the re-embedding on a GPU machine, see Switching the embedding model.

docker-compose.selfhost.yml already points PAPER_FEED_DIR (/app/data/feed) and VECTOR_STORE_DIR (/app/data/vectors) at the paper_files volume, so both survive a rebuild. If you run the backend some other way, put both folders (and CONFERENCE_DATA_DIR) on a persistent disk.

docs.title: Step 3b: run on Heroku
docs.text:
Heroku has no free tier and no persistent disk, so the database lives on Neo4j AuraDB Free.

  1. Create an AuraDB Free instance at console.neo4j.io. Save the generated password. Note the connection URI (neo4j+s://xxxx.databases.neo4j.io).
  2. Create the app and switch it to container builds:
heroku login
heroku create <app-name>                  # e.g. papers-alex → https://papers-alex-xxxx.herokuapp.com
heroku stack:set container -a <app-name>
  1. Set the configuration. Use the same values as in .env, plus the Heroku-specific ones:
APP_HOST=<app-name>-xxxx.herokuapp.com    # the host from `heroku apps:info -a <app-name>`
heroku config:set -a <app-name> \
  NEO4J_URI='neo4j+s://xxxx.databases.neo4j.io' NEO4J_USER=neo4j NEO4J_PASSWORD='<aura password>' \
  JWT_SECRET_KEY="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" DEFAULT_USER_NAME='<your login name>' \
  ANTHROPIC_API_KEY='sk-ant-...' \
  GOOGLE_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID='<folder id>' \
  GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID='<client_id from credentials.json>' \
  GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET='<client_secret from credentials.json>' \
  GOOGLE_TOKEN_JSON="$(cat backend/token.json)" \
  DOCLING_MODE=local INFERENCE_MANAGER_URL= HERMIONE_HOST= LITELLM_ENDPOINT= LITELLM_EMBED_MODEL= \
  FRONTEND_URL="https://$APP_HOST" TRUSTED_HOSTS="$APP_HOST" TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true

Heroku has no disk to keep token.json on, so GOOGLE_TOKEN_JSON passes its contents as a variable. GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET are inside backend/credentials.json.

  1. Deploy. heroku.yml makes Heroku build Dockerfile.selfhost:
git push heroku main
heroku ps:type web=standard-2x -a <app-name>   # 1 GB RAM; basic (512 MB) runs out of memory
heroku logs --tail -a <app-name>               # wait for "Application startup complete"

If a PDF upload crashes with "Memory quota exceeded" in the logs, the layout model needs more memory. Use performance-m. Heroku also cuts every request off after 30 seconds (error H12). Long PDFs can take longer than that to process, so very large uploads may fail on Heroku even though they work locally.

  1. Create your account (step 4), then open https://<APP_HOST>.

To update: git pull from GitHub, then git push heroku main again.

Heroku's disk is wiped at every restart. The vectors of the library search are then rebuilt on the CPU (search answers by keywords until that is done) and the paper feed would lose its ratings and fetched papers, so leave PAPER_FEED off there.

docs.title: Step 4: create your account
docs.text:
The account named DEFAULT_USER_NAME is the owner and admin. It is also the only account that uses the server-wide ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Other users you add later enter their own key under Settings.

# localhost
docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml exec app python scripts/create_default_user.py
# Heroku
heroku run -a <app-name> python scripts/create_default_user.py

The script asks for a password (at least 8 characters).

Log in, then follow First steps to add your first paper and try the tour, the concept map and the chat.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause / fix 400 Invalid host header TRUSTED_HOSTS must list the exact host name you open in the browser Login works but every page says "Session expired" The page and the API are on different origins. Open the app on the URL you set as FRONTEND_URL Upload fails with Drive upload failed token.json is missing or expired, or GOOGLE_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID is wrong. Re-run step 2.5 (on Heroku, update GOOGLE_TOKEN_JSON) Upload hangs or the dyno restarts Out of memory in the Docling layout model: give the container more RAM ServiceUnavailable / Neo4j errors at start Locally, Neo4j needs ~30 s after the first start; the app retries on restart. On Heroku, check NEO4J_URI uses neo4j+s:// Chat says "Personal Anthropic key is not configured" Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and log in as the DEFAULT_USER_NAME account (or enter a key under Settings)

docs.title: PaperManager — UI Style Guide
docs.text: Single source of truth for all frontend styling decisions. Tokens are defined in frontend/src/index.css via Tailwind v4 @theme. When in doubt, use a semantic token instead of a raw Tailwind color.

docs.title: 1. Design Tokens
docs.text: These are the only colors you should use for structure and text. They map to fixed Tailwind values and support future theming (e.g. dark mode) by changing one place.

All modals share the same structural shell:

    </div>

    <div className="px-6 py-4 border-t border-line-s flex justify-end gap-2">

Multi-step modals add a StepDots component above the subtitle:

function StepDots({ current, total }: { current: number; total: number }) {
  return (
    <div className="flex gap-1 items-center">
      {Array.from({ length: total }).map((_, i) => (
        <span key={i} className={`w-1.5 h-1.5 rounded-full transition-colors ${
          i === current ? "bg-accent" : i < current ? "bg-violet-300" : "bg-line"
        }`} />
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

docs.title: AI Pipelines
docs.text: PaperManager uses multiple AI models for different tasks. This page documents each pipeline, the models used, and how they fit together.

docs.title: Models Used
docs.text:
Model Provider Used for claude-opus-4-6 Anthropic Paper summarisation, single-paper chat, knowledge chat, cross-paper synthesis, research gap analysis claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 Anthropic Abstract extraction, reference extraction, topic suggestion, claim extraction, chapter summarisation, conversation compaction, figure captioning (claude-vision mode) llama3.2:3b Ollama (local) Metadata extraction (layer 2), tag suggestion, chapter detection, figure captions (default), affiliation extraction, Cypher assist, merge scan BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (default of EMBED_MODEL) local, CPU (transformers) Embedding vectors of titles and abstracts for library semantic search, the paper feed, similar papers and the conference explorer LITELLM_EMBED_MODEL (empty = off) LiteLLM proxy Legacy Paper.embedding vector used by the knowledge chat's semantic tool

All Anthropic calls can be routed through an enterprise Foundry gateway by setting ANTHROPIC_WORK_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_WORK_BASE_URL.

docs.title: Metadata Extraction Pipeline (PDF Upload)
docs.text:
Runs when a PDF is uploaded. Tries strategies in order, stopping at the first success:

flowchart TD
    Start["PDF bytes"] --> Extract["Docling extracts raw_text"]
    Extract --> FindDOI{DOI / arXiv ID\nfound in text?}

    FindDOI -->|"Yes"| S2["Layer 1a: Semantic Scholar API"]
    S2 -->|fail| CR["Layer 1a fallback: CrossRef API"]

    FindDOI -->|"No DOI but\ntitle found"| S2Title["Layer 1b: S2 title search"]

    FindDOI -->|"Nothing found"| Ollama["Layer 2: Ollama llama3.2:3b\non first 3 000 chars"]
    Ollama -->|"Ollama unavailable"| Heuristic["Layer 3: Regex heuristics\n(first line = title, year regex)"]

    S2 --> AbstractCheck{Abstract\nextracted?}
    CR --> AbstractCheck
    S2Title --> AbstractCheck
    Ollama --> AbstractCheck
    Heuristic --> AbstractCheck

    AbstractCheck -->|"No"| AbstractFallback["ABSTRACT_RE regex\n→ Claude Haiku if regex fails"]
    AbstractCheck -->|"Yes"| Done["Metadata ready"]
    AbstractFallback --> Done
Layer Trigger Service Output 1a (primary) DOI or arXiv ID in text Semantic Scholar API title, year, authors, abstract, topics, citation count, venue 1a (fallback) S2 fails CrossRef API title, year, authors, doi, venue 1b Title found, no DOI S2 title search same as 1a 2 No DOI, no useful title Ollama llama3.2:3b on raw_text[:3000] title, year, authors (structured JSON) 3 Ollama unavailable Regex on raw_text title (first non-empty line), year (4-digit year regex) Abstract fallback Abstract still missing ABSTRACT_RE regex → Claude Haiku abstract text

The metadata_source property on the Paper node records which layer was used.

docs.title: Reference Extraction Pipeline
docs.text:
Triggered via GET /papers/{id}/extract-references or POST /papers/{id}/references.

flowchart TD
    Start["Paper with raw_text"] --> P["Parser over every reference section\n(count = yardstick)"]
    P --> A{DOI / arXiv id?}
    A -->|"Yes"| S2["A: Semantic Scholar /references"]
    S2 -->|"≥ 80% of parser count"| Done["Reference list"]
    S2 -->|"short or none"| LLM["B: LLM over the section\n6k-char chunks, LiteLLM then Claude"]
    A -->|"No"| LLM
    LLM -->|"≥ 80%"| Vet["Identifier check\n(citecheck: doi.org, arXiv API)"]
    LLM -->|"short"| Best["C: longest of S2 / LLM / parser"]
    Best -->|"LLM or parser"| Vet
    Best -->|"S2"| Done
    Vet --> Done

Identifier check. Before a list from the LLM or the parser is shown, every DOI and arXiv id in it is resolved (services/citecheck.py, no model): doi.org content negotiation returns the registered title, the arXiv API answers 100 ids per request, 16 lookups run in parallel within a 60 s budget. Dead ids are dropped; an id whose registered title does not match the extracted one is dropped too (LLMs invent and misremember ids, the parser can pick up the next entry's id), unless the parser's "title" is an author fragment, in which case the registered title replaces it. Each reference carries id_check. scripts/check_reference_ids.py runs the same check over existing stubs.

Each reference creates a Paper stub node tagged from-references and linked via CITES. Stubs are enriched when the full paper is later imported.

docs.title: Claim Extraction
docs.text:
Triggered automatically during upload (for papers) or via POST /papers/{id}/claims/extract.

flowchart LR
    A["raw_text + title"] --> P["Load prompts/claims.txt"]
    P --> C["Claude Haiku"]
    C --> Claims["List of {text, type} claims"]
    Claims --> DB["Create Claim nodes\nHAS_CLAIM relationships"]

Claim types include "finding", "method", "limitation", "contribution".

docs.title: Embeddings and the vector store
docs.text:
No language-model call is made. A local embedder (transformers on the CPU, services/conferences/embedder.py) turns the title and abstract of every paper (or its summary when there is no abstract) into a unit vector. The model is EMBED_MODEL, by default BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (384 numbers per paper); services/vectorstore/model_config.py holds the dimension, pooling and prefixes of the models it knows and takes EMBED_DIM and friends for others.

flowchart LR
    A["title + abstract"] --> E["Embedder (CPU)\nEMBED_MODEL"]
    E --> S["Vector store\nnamespaces: library, feed, feed_library"]
    S --> L["Library search\n(hybrid / semantic)"]
    S --> F["Paper feed ranking"]
    S --> M["Similar papers\nPOST /search/similar, MCP"]

Each namespace records the model it was built with, so vectors of two models are never mixed: after an EMBED_MODEL change, search answers by keywords until the namespace is rebuilt on the CPU in the background, or until a generation prepared elsewhere is adopted on start (scripts/vectors_export.py, embed_bulk.py on a GPU machine, vectors_import.py; vectors_rollback.py goes back). The conference explorer keeps its own saved vectors and reads CONFERENCE_EMBED_MODEL first. See Switching the embedding model and .specs/019_vector_store.md.

The optional paper feed trains a small numpy logistic regression per user on these vectors (no API call) and similar papers is a nearest-neighbour search over the same namespaces.

The older Paper.embedding (a 768-dim vector with the Neo4j index paper_embeddings) is produced through the LiteLLM embeddings API with LITELLM_EMBED_MODEL, which is empty by default (off). Only the knowledge chat's semantic tool uses it; it fails silently when unavailable.

docs.title: Single-Paper Chat
docs.text:
Triggered via POST /papers/{id}/chat.

The model is selected per-request: Claude Opus (default), Claude Work (enterprise gateway), or Ollama.

docs.title: Chapter Detection (Books / Lecture Decks)
docs.text:
Triggered via POST /papers/{id}/chapters/detect.

flowchart TD
    PDF["PDF from Google Drive"] --> Docling["Strategy 1: Docling\nstructural chapter detection"]
    Docling -->|"found chapters"| Done["Create Chapter nodes"]
    Docling -->|"no chapters"| Regex["Strategy 2: Regex\non raw_text headings"]
    Regex -->|"found chapters"| Done
    Regex -->|"no chapters"| AI["Strategy 3: Ollama AI\n(use_ai=true only)"]
    AI --> Done
    Done --> Summarize["Ollama summarizes\neach chapter"]

Each chapter node stores its text slice, title, level, page range, and summary.

Chapter chat uses prompts/chapter_chat_system.txt with Claude Haiku; chapter summary uses prompts/chapter_summary.txt with Ollama.

docs.text:
Triggered via POST /papers/{id}/figures/extract.

flowchart TD

    Docling --> Method{Caption method\nfrom settings}
    Method -->|"docling"| DocCaption["Docling structural caption"]
    Method -->|"ollama"| OllamaCaption["Ollama llama3.2:3b\nfrom prompts/figure_captions.txt"]

    DocCaption --> Upload["Upload PNG to Google Drive"]
    OllamaCaption --> Upload
    ClaudeCaption --> Upload
    Upload --> DB["Save Figure node in Neo4j"]

docs.title: Cross-Paper Synthesis
docs.text:
Triggered via POST /synthesis.

flowchart LR
    Q["paper_ids + question"] --> Papers["Fetch Paper nodes"]
    Papers --> P["Load prompts/synthesis.txt"]
    P --> C["Claude Opus\n(+ optional web search)"]
    C --> R["Synthesis text"]

docs.title: Research Gap Analysis
docs.text:
Triggered via POST /research-gaps.

flowchart LR
    Q["topic + paper_ids / project_id"] --> Papers["Fetch relevant papers"]
    Papers --> P["Load prompts/research_gaps.txt"]
    P --> C["Claude Opus\n(+ optional web search)"]
    C --> R["Gap analysis text"]

docs.title: Knowledge Chat Context Assembly
docs.text:
Triggered via POST /knowledge-chat/stream.

flowchart TD
    Q["User question"] --> Parse["Parse @mentions\n@tag:, @topic:, @project:, @paper:"]
    Parse -->|"Mentions found"| Cypher["Run Cypher queries\nto fetch matching papers"]
    Parse -->|"No mentions"| Recent["Fetch 10 most recently\nadded papers"]
    Cypher --> Budget["Apply token budget\nper paper (truncate raw_text)"]
    Recent --> Budget
    Budget --> System["Load prompts/knowledge_chat_system.txt"]
    System --> Claude["Claude Opus 4.6\n(streaming SSE)"]
    Claude --> Browser["Token-by-token response"]

The model also has library tools (graph queries, semantic search, a paper's full text, its figures, web search). Each tool call is streamed to the browser as a step event and saved with the answer, so the chat shows what was looked up; the papers a call touched feed the Sources row. The system prompt ends with an instruction that lets the model append one <suggestion>...</suggestion> line when the session shows a gap in PaperManager itself. services/suggestions.py strips that tag from the token stream (whatever the token boundaries), so neither the browser nor the saved message contains it, then records the suggestion (merging it into an open or planned one with the same normalised text or a word-set overlap of 0.75) and emits a suggestion event. SUGGESTIONS_FROM_CHAT=false keeps stripping but records nothing.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
POST /reports creates a Report node (status queued) and hands it to a background thread pool (REPORTS_MAX_PARALLEL, default 2). services/reports/pipeline.py then runs, checking a cancel flag between steps:

flowchart LR
    S["Scope<br/>10 %"] --> P["Plan<br/>20 %"] --> E["Evidence<br/>55 %"] --> Sec["Sections<br/>90 %"] --> F["Frame<br/>97 %"] --> V["Save<br/>100 %"]
  1. Scope. Candidates are the papers given, the project's papers, and the top hits of the library search for the question (hybrid mode, visibility-filtered as the requesting user). A project with no question asks for an overview of the project's literature.
  2. Plan. One JSON call (prompts/report_plan.txt): title, lede and 3, 5 or 7 sections (short, standard, long), each with a focus, one to three search queries and the candidate papers it should draw on.
  3. Evidence. Per section, extra retrieval with its queries, then an evidence pack per paper (up to 8 per section): title, year, authors, venue, summary, abstract, up to 8 claims, your note, up to 6 highlights with comments and up to 2 full-text passages around the query terms. Packs are capped by a character budget (REPORTS_EVIDENCE_CHARS; by default 20,000 on the LiteLLM model, 60,000 on Anthropic or OpenAI). Each paper gets a source number S1...Sn.
  4. Sections. One call per section (prompts/report_section.txt) in Markdown; every claim is followed by an [S3] marker and only the section's own sources may be cited.
  5. Frame. One call (prompts/report_frame.txt): the introduction and a closing section (what the library shows, what it does not, open questions).
  6. Save. Markers become [[3]](/paper/<id>) links, unknown markers are dropped, a reference list is appended in order of first citation and a CITES_PAPER edge is written per cited paper.

Models: fast (default; the server's fast provider: LiteLLM, Claude Haiku or OpenAI), claude (your personal key, REPORTS_CLAUDE_MODEL, default claude-sonnet-4-6) and claude-work (the work gateway). A restart marks queued and running reports failed. All calls run inside usage_context(feature="reports", user=owner), so the usage ledger attributes the cost. The HTML export (render.py) is one self-contained page; Markdown is the stored text.

docs.title: Usage Ledger
docs.text: Every call in every pipeline above is recorded without the pipeline knowing: the SDK methods are wrapped once and the feature name is derived from the calling code (summary, topics, claims, knowledge-chat, concepts, tour, reports, ...). See Architecture.

The keyword list in prompts/literature_search_keywords.txt (or a project's stored keywords) is used to query arXiv, PubMed, and bioRxiv. Results are streamed via SSE and marked as already-in-library where applicable.

Parameter Type Description q string Query: words (prefix, one typo for 5+ letters), "phrases", word*, a DOI or arXiv id. Case and accents are ignored tag string Filter by tag name (case-insensitive) topic string Filter by topic name (case-insensitive) project_id string Filter by project ID person_id string Filter by person ID (authored or involved) venue string Filter by venue (case-insensitive) year_min int Minimum publication year year_max int Maximum publication year reading_status string Filter by reading status bookmarked bool Only bookmarked papers added_after string Added on or after YYYY-MM-DD or an ISO datetime; a bad value returns 422 added_before string Added before YYYY-MM-DD (that day included) or an ISO datetime; 422 on a bad value has_pdf, has_text, has_note, has_highlights bool PDF stored, full text extracted, a note exists, at least one highlight document_type string paper, book, lecture_deck or news_article rating_min int Minimum star rating, 1–5 include_references bool Include reference stubs (tag from-references); default true, ranked below library papers mode string lexical (default), hybrid (lexical + embedding similarity, reciprocal-rank fusion) or semantic; falls back to lexical while the embedding index is not ready sort string relevance (default with q), date_desc (default without), date_asc, year_desc, year_asc, title_asc, rating_desc, citations_desc, updated_desc snippets int Passages per hit, 0–6 (default 2) skip, limit int Paging after ranking; limit 1–2000 (default 20)

Response: {results, total, mode, relaxed, semantic, failed_sources, took_ms}. total counts every hit, not just the page. Each hit is the paper plus score, matched_in (coarse, e.g. note+paper), matched_fields (doi, title, author, topic, tag, venue, abstract, summary, note, highlight, claim, fulltext, semantic), matches (matched author / topic / tag / venue names), snippets ({field, text, marks, page?}), title_marks, authors, is_reference, similarity (hybrid/semantic), text_chars, has_note, highlight_count, projects. marks are [start, end) offsets in code points. relaxed: true means no paper contained every word and partial matches are shown. Ranking, weights and indexes: .specs/012_search.md. Ranked results are cached in-process for 60 s per user (any non-GET request clears the cache; LIBRARY_SEARCH_CACHE=0 turns it off).

docs.title: The Shared Layer Principle
docs.text:
The most important architectural rule in PaperManager:

db/queries/ and services/ are framework-neutral. Neither FastAPI nor MCP specifics leak into them. routers/ and tools/ are two different entry points over the same logic.

This means every capability is available both via HTTP (for the browser) and via MCP tool calls (for Claude Desktop), without any code duplication.

docs.title: Usage Ledger
docs.text:
Every call to a language model is recorded once, in a SQLite file (USAGE_DB_PATH, default backend/data/usage.sqlite), and read by the Tokens page and the Health page. SQLite and not Neo4j: the ledger is append-only, grows by a row per call (thousands a day during a bulk import), is only read as aggregates, and keeps working when the graph is down.

graph LR
    Call["Any call site<br/>services/, routers/"] --> SDK["anthropic / openai SDK<br/>(wrapped once)"]
    SDK --> Hook["services/usage/hook.py<br/>feature, user, paper, cost"]
    CC["Claude Code CLI<br/>(subprocess)"] -->|"explicit record"| Hook
    Hook --> Ledger[("usage.sqlite<br/>table llm_calls")]
    Ledger --> Tokens["/tokens/*"]
    Ledger --> Health["/system/health"]
  • No call site has to remember it. usage.install() runs once when main.py is imported and wraps, at class level, Messages.create / Messages.stream (also the beta variants) of anthropic and Completions.create and Embeddings.create of openai. That covers the personal key, the work gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and every future client. The MCP server calls install_lazy() so its start-up stays free of both SDKs. Claude Code runs the CLI in a subprocess and records its result explicitly.
  • Attribution. An explicit usage_context(feature=, user=, paper_id=) wins. Otherwise the feature is derived from the innermost backend frame on the call stack through a rules table (hook.FEATURE_RULES), the user from the request (copied into worker threads), the paper from a paper_id local. Background work (sweepers, ingest workers) has no user.
  • Cost. One price table (USD per million tokens, longest model-prefix match; extra rows via USAGE_PRICES_FILE). LiteLLM costs 0, Claude Code reports its own list-price equivalent, an unknown model is stored with no price and flagged. Streams are recorded at the end; without reported usage the tokens are estimated and marked.
  • Safety. Recording never raises into the call path; USAGE_LEDGER_ENABLED=false turns it off.

Row layout and API: .specs/013_tokens.md.

docs.title: Embeddings and the vector store
docs.text:
Everything that compares papers by meaning (library semantic search, the optional paper feed, similar papers, the conference explorer) uses one CPU embedder and one vector store, not Neo4j.

graph LR
    Embedder["Embedder (CPU)<br/>EMBED_MODEL"] --> Store[("Vector store<br/>VECTOR_STORE_DIR")]
    Store --> Search["Library search"]
    Store --> Feed["Paper feed<br/>(+ feed.sqlite)"]
    Store --> Similar["Similar papers<br/>/search/similar, MCP"]
    MCP["MCP server"] -->|"POST /conferences/embed"| Embedder
  • One model setting. services/vectorstore/model_config.py reads EMBED_MODEL (default BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, 384 numbers per paper) and, for a model it does not know, EMBED_DIM, EMBED_POOLING and the prefixes. The conference explorer keeps its own saved vectors and reads CONFERENCE_EMBED_MODEL first.
  • Never mixed. Each namespace (library, feed, feed_library) records the model it was built with. When the configured model differs the namespace is stale: search falls back to keywords while it is rebuilt in the background, or a generation prepared on a GPU machine is adopted on start (scripts/vectors_export.py, embed_bulk.py, vectors_import.py; vectors_rollback.py goes back). See Switching the embedding model.
  • Backends. numpy on a memory-mapped file plus SQLite by default; LanceDB is optional (VECTOR_STORE=lance).
  • The MCP server loads no model. It reads the stores read-only and asks the backend for query vectors (POST /conferences/embed, PM_EMBED_URL), so it needs the same VECTOR_STORE_DIR (and PAPER_FEED_DIR) as the backend.

Developer notes: .specs/019_vector_store.md.

docs.title: Key Design Decisions
docs.text:
See the full Decisions Log for rationale. The key principles:

  1. Neo4j over SQL — papers, people, topics, and tags are naturally a graph
  2. Tags as nodes — (Paper)-[:TAGGED]->(Tag) allows efficient "all papers with tag X" queries
  3. Topic ≠ Tag — Topics are formal research areas; Tags are free-form personal labels
  4. Notes as graph nodes — Notes have their own @mention and #topic relationships
  5. Shared service layer — MCP tools and HTTP routers call the same db/ and services/ code
  6. Prompts as files — All prompt templates live in prompts/ and are loaded fresh on each call
  7. Vector embeddings outside the graph — library search, the paper feed and similar papers read one vector store that records the embedding model of each index (default BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, CPU); the model can be switched with a rebuild or a GPU bulk job, and vectors of two models are never mixed
  8. User identity — User nodes enable per-user conversation history and attribution
  9. Ledger outside the graph — LLM usage is bookkeeping, not library content, so it lives in SQLite

docs.title: main.py — App Entry Point
docs.text:
main.py creates the FastAPI application, sets up CORS, registers all routers, and defines a startup lifespan:

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    get_driver().verify_connectivity()   # verify Neo4j
    run_schema_setup(get_driver())       # create indexes + constraints
    seed_default_tags(get_driver())      # seed default tags
    seed_people_tags(get_driver())       # seed people-related tags
    recover_interrupted(get_driver())    # mark reports left running by a restart as failed
    yield

The app is started by start.sh via uvicorn backend.main:app.

docs.title: db/schema.py — Constraints and Indexes
docs.text:
Runs on startup. Creates:

  • Uniqueness constraints on: Paper.id, Person.id, Topic.id, Topic.name, Tag.id, Tag.name, Note.id, Project.id, Figure.id, Annotation.id, Blog.id, BlogPost.id, User.id, User.name, Claim.id, Table.id, Conversation.id, Message.id, Venue.id, Report.id, Suggestion.id
  • Fulltext indexes: paper_search (title, abstract, summary), note_search (content), annotation_search (highlighted_text, note), claim_search (text), entity_name_search (Person/Topic/Tag/Project name), paper_text_search (venue, raw_text) with the standard-folding analyzer (rebuilt at startup if their analyzer or fields differ; see .specs/012_search.md), and message_search (content)
  • Range indexes on Paper.created_at, Paper.year and Paper.updated_at (paper_created_at, paper_year, paper_updated_at), for the date, year and sort filters of the Library
  • Vector index: paper_embeddings on Paper.embedding (768-dim cosine; filled only when LITELLM_EMBED_MODEL is set); not used by library search, which keeps its vectors in the vector store (services/vectorstore/, .specs/019_vector_store.md)

docs.title: Embedding benchmark
docs.text:
How the embedding models compared on one real library, and how to run the same comparison on yours. It backs the advice in Switching the embedding model. The default model is still BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5; nothing here changes it.

Short version. On this library, citation-neighbour recall was higher for larger and for scientific-paper embedders than for the small default, by about 0.03 to 0.09 (standard error about 0.02), and the ranking among the top models was not stable between two runs. The feed's AUC did not separate the models. Treat the table as a starting point for your own run, not as a recommendation.

docs.title: Run it on your own library
docs.text:
python backend/scripts/embedder_benchmark.py --data <export dir> --models <id1,id2,...> --out <results dir> --device cuda

The script embeds your library and the feed candidates with each model (one process per model, fp16 on a GPU) and writes the metrics below. Its docstring lists the export format and the model-specific layouts. Keep the export and the results out of the git repository: they contain your library.

This is an anonymised summary of an offline benchmark of text-embedding models on one personal PaperManager library. No paper titles, ids, topic names, user names or hosts appear here. The benchmark script is backend/scripts/embedder_benchmark.py; the exact data are private.

docs.title: Dataset
docs.text:
run 1 run 2 (this run) library papers (real, not reference stubs) 1,341 1,342 of these with an abstract 604 1,181 with an abstract or an AI summary 612 1,184 citation edges between library papers 345 345 library papers with at least one such edge (excluding self-citations) 192 192 of these with an abstract (strict subset) not measured 189 library papers with at least one topic 459 468 reference stubs with an abstract (extra neighbour pool) not used 5,321 of 9,749 feed candidates (arXiv and bioRxiv preprints) 2,325 2,958

Between the runs, abstracts were back-filled for most real papers and for about half of the reference stubs. The citation graph among real papers did not change. The live system also switched its embedding model to SciEmbed full between the runs, so run 2 is the first run on the final texts.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Text: title, newline, abstract (or AI summary when there is no abstract) cut to 1,500 characters; the same text the application embeds. Models whose card asks for it get their own layout (title [SEP] abstract for SPECTER2 and SciNCL, a title/abstract pair for MedCPT, a document prefix for Nomic). Max length 512 tokens, fp16 on a GPU, unit-normalised vectors, pooling per model card (CLS, mean or last token). Each model ran in its own process. The two models with custom code (GTE-large, Nomic) ran with remote code allowed, for this benchmark only, on transformers 4.57.
  • M1, citation-neighbour recall: for every paper with at least one citation edge inside the pool, take its 10 nearest neighbours by cosine (itself excluded); recall@10 is the share of its cited and citing papers found; MRR is the reciprocal rank of the first cited or citing paper in the full ranking. Variants: all = all 192 real papers with an edge (pool: the 1,342 real papers); strict = only the 189 queries that have a real abstract (pool unchanged); stubs = the 281 real papers with at least one edge to any pool paper as queries, and a pool of all 6,663 papers (1,342 real + 5,321 reference stubs with text; stubs without any text are left out), 7,556 citation edges. Random-neighbour baseline recall@10 is 0.008 (all) and 0.002 (stubs pool).
  • M2, topic agreement: mean Jaccard overlap of the topic sets of a paper and its 10 nearest library neighbours, over the 468 papers that have topics. Random-neighbour baseline: 0.010.
  • M3, feed classifier AUC: the feed's own training and evaluation code is run on each model's vectors (positives from the user's ratings, reads and additions; the feed candidates as random negatives). "feed" is the number the live feed reports: the 20 % most recently added positives held out (23 of 117 positives). "random" holds out a random 20 % of the positives instead (also 23 of 117), repeated for three seeds; the table gives mean (standard deviation over seeds).
  • Throughput is papers per second over all 9,621 texts (library, candidates, stubs) with the model already loaded, on a GPU shared with unrelated jobs; peak memory is torch's peak allocated GPU memory.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
• M1 (all and strict): Qwen3-Embedding-4B has the highest recall (0.372 strict, 0.088 above the bge-small baseline with a paired standard error of 0.021). SciEmbed full, GTE-large and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B follow (strict 0.339, 0.338, 0.326; paired gaps to the baseline of 0.056, 0.054, 0.043, standard errors 0.019 to 0.022). bge-base is +0.034 (SE 0.015). MedCPT is clearly lowest (0.211), below the baseline (0.283), as expected for a biomedical-only encoder.
  • M1 with the stubs pool: absolute recall is lower (0.10 to 0.17) because each query now has many more cited papers to find in a pool five times larger. SciEmbed full is best (0.170), then ctx-8192 (0.166), Qwen3-4B (0.165), ctx-2048 (0.162); the baseline is 0.138. The model ranking is moderately stable across pools (Spearman 0.75 between "all" and "stubs"); the main change is that the three SciEmbed models move up and GTE-large and bge-large move down. Qwen3-4B has the best MRR (0.546) in the stubs pool.
  • M2: every model is far above the random baseline (0.010) but they differ little (0.064 to 0.071), except MedCPT (0.056). GTE-large and SciEmbed full are the highest (0.071).
  • M3: very noisy. With the feed's temporal hold-out (23 positives) the AUCs spread from 0.47 to 0.70 with no consistent order across the two runs (Spearman 0.60 between runs). bge-m3 is highest (0.704) and Qwen3-4B next (0.645) there. With random hold-outs the three seeds of one model range by up to 0.12 (for example 0.79 to 0.92 for the baseline); means are 0.85 to 0.91, with bge-m3, MedCPT, Qwen3-4B and the SciEmbed models at the top. Differences between neighbouring models in M3 are within noise.

  • The text changed a lot (abstracts for 1,181 instead of 604 papers), but M1 and M2 changed little. M1 recall moved by up to about 0.03 per model (the baseline fell from 0.292 to 0.279, SciEmbed full from 0.360 to 0.334, Qwen3-0.6B rose from 0.297 to 0.321). The M2 ranking is practically unchanged (Spearman 0.98) and the M1 ranking moderately so (0.70). In run 1 SciEmbed full led M1 outright; in run 2 it is within noise of Qwen3-4B, GTE-large and Qwen3-0.6B, and Qwen3-4B (not run before) is ahead on the strict subset.
  • The feed-style M3 AUC fell for most models, including the baseline (0.576 to 0.474), and its ranking changed (Spearman 0.60). The held-out set is 23 positives in both runs and the library, the candidate set (2,958 instead of 2,325 papers) and the training set (117 instead of 113 positives) all changed, so this is consistent with noise and a different candidate mix; no cause was tested. The random-hold-out AUC rose slightly for nearly all models and the ordering is stable (Spearman 0.87).
  • Throughput roughly doubled for most models (Nomic got slower, 188 to 148 papers/s); the GPU load from other jobs differed between runs, so throughput is not comparable across runs.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• M1 and M2 measure agreement with this one user's own citation graph and topic labels, not usefulness for search or recommendations. The graph is small (345 edges).
  • The standard error of an M1 recall mean is about 0.02, so gaps below about 0.04 between models are not distinguishable. Queries in the "stubs" variant differ from the other variants, so absolute values are not comparable across variants.
  • M3 has 23 held-out positives and the random-hold-out numbers measure mostly whether a model separates the user's papers from recent preprints. It is not a measure of ranking quality inside the feed.
  • Only 3 seeds, one library, one run per model; fp16 throughput numbers come from a shared GPU.

docs.title: Library (Library.tsx)
docs.text: Main landing page. One sticky bar holds the search box, the Filters popover (components/search/FilterMenu.tsx; a bottom sheet on phones), the add button and the ⋯ menu. All query and filter state lives in the URL (filterState.ts, pure and unit-tested). Without a query it shows Continue reading and Recently added, loaded one page at a time; with a query, ranked rows with matched-in chips.

docs.title: PaperDetail (PaperDetail.tsx)
docs.text:
Single paper view with:

  • Metadata panel (left): title, authors, year, tags, topics, people, rating
  • Tab panel (center): PDF viewer, Figures, Notes (NoteEditor), References, Chapters, Claims, Annotations
  • Chat panel (right): single-paper Q&A (ChatPanel)

docs.title: Graph (Graph.tsx)
docs.text: Uses force-graph (WebGL) to render the knowledge graph. Fetches from GET /graph?mode=.... Clicking a node opens EntityPanel for details. For admins, Query opens components/graph/CypherPanel.tsx: one POST /graph/query run feeds a Graph tab (drawn in the main canvas) and a Table tab (ResultTable); examples, saved queries (localStorage), schema and AI assist live there too.

docs.title: KnowledgeChat (KnowledgeChat.tsx)
docs.text: Multi-paper AI chat, laid out like the desk chat. Sends messages to POST /knowledge-chat/stream (SSE) and renders each event as it arrives: step events become ToolCall rows, interim text the model's notes between them, token the answer, suggestion a SuggestionChip. Under an answer: TurnSources (papers it cited, read or searched), FigureStrip with a lightbox, concept cards, structure cards (kchat/structure/, 3Dmol.js; PDB, AlphaFold DB, ligands by CCD or PubChem) and KaTeX maths with copy-as-TeX (copyTex.ts). Stop calls POST /knowledge-chat/stop; retry re-asks. Supports @tag:, @topic:, @project:, @paper:, @person:, @user: mentions to scope context.

docs.title: LiteratureSearch (LiteratureSearch.tsx)
docs.text: Streams recent papers from arXiv, PubMed, and bioRxiv using keyword lists. Papers can be added to the library in one click.

docs.title: Find papers (Discover folded in)
docs.text: LiteratureSearch.tsx has two tabs: Search (components/literature/ExternalSearch.tsx: arXiv, Semantic Scholar, PubMed and bioRxiv, showing which results are already in the library) and Feed (KeywordFeed.tsx). The old Discover page is gone.

docs.title: Paper feed (Feed.tsx) and Similar papers (SimilarSearch.tsx)
docs.text: Both sit under Explore. Feed.tsx (/feed, API in api/feed.ts) shows the setup panel until the user has chosen categories, then the ranked list with a status strip (FeedStatus, whose ranking line comes from modeText.ts: a trained model, similarity to the library, or newest first); rows are FeedRow. The nav entry exists only when the instance has the feed on: lib/features.ts asks GET /feed/status once after login. SimilarSearch.tsx (/similar, api/similar.ts) posts a title and paragraph to POST /search/similar, shows scope buttons only when the feed is on, and lists SimilarRows; Use this paper as the query copies a hit's text into the box (queryFromHit.ts). Both are lazy-loaded.

docs.title: Tokens, Reports, Suggestions, Health
docs.text: Four pages over the same small kit (components/insights/, API in api/insights.ts). Tokens.tsx reads /tokens/summary, /tokens/calls and /tokens/prices; Reports.tsx and ReportView.tsx poll /reports while a report runs and offer Markdown and HTML export; Suggestions.tsx lists, votes and (admins) sets status; Health.tsx reads /system/health (admin only, refresh button).
