docs.title: Paper feed
docs.text:
The Paper feed (Explore → Paper feed, /feed) is a digest of new preprints from arXiv, bioRxiv and medRxiv, ranked for you by what you already keep in your library. It is optional and off by default: the menu entry does not exist until the person who runs the server switches it on.

(Not to be confused with the Feed tab of Explore → Find papers, which streams recent papers for keywords you type; the paper feed here is chosen by arXiv category and ranked by your library.)

Open the feed once a day, look at the top of the list, add what you want with one click, and tell it what it got wrong. Every thumbs-up and thumbs-down makes the next ranking a little better.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
The server owner sets one variable in .env and restarts the backend:

PAPER_FEED=true

With PAPER_FEED=false (the default) nothing runs: no background thread, no folder, no model, no request to any other server, and the feed's API answers not found. The other settings are in .env.example:

Variable Default Meaning PAPER_FEED false Master switch PAPER_FEED_DIR /data/feed Where the feed keeps its small database (feed.sqlite) PAPER_FEED_INTERVAL 21600 Seconds between refreshes (6 hours) PAPER_FEED_RETENTION_DAYS 30 How long fetched papers are kept (papers you rated are kept) PAPER_FEED_MAX_PER_REFRESH 2000 Most papers fetched per source and refresh PAPER_FEED_CONTACT empty Optional contact (an address or a URL) added to the User-Agent that arXiv and bioRxiv see, so they can reach you if your instance misbehaves

The papers the feed has fetched are called candidates on this and the other pages. They are embedded with the same model as the library search and similar papers: EMBED_MODEL, by default BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (384 numbers per paper) on the CPU. No GPU, no API key and no extra package is needed. If the operator changes the model, see Switching the embedding model; the feed's ranking retrains by itself afterwards.

docs.title: Choosing what you see
docs.text:
The first time you open the page it asks what the feed should show:

  • Sources. arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv. bioRxiv and medRxiv have no categories: you get every new preprint and the ranking puts the relevant ones first.
  • arXiv categories. Type names such as cs.LG, cs.CV or q-bio.BM, or click an example. arXiv has too many papers to fetch everything, so the feed fetches only the categories you choose, and nothing at all until someone has chosen one. The arXiv category list shows every name.
  • Digest window. How many days back the list reaches (1 to 14, default 3).

You can change this later with Settings in the status strip. Each person on the instance has their own choices, ratings and ranking; the server fetches the union of what everybody chose.

docs.title: Reading the list
docs.text:
Each row shows the title (it opens the preprint), authors, date, a relevance bar, why (the three papers in your library it is closest to) and the abstract on a click. The buttons:

  • Add to library ingests the paper the same way pasting its link on the Library page does. Add to project does the same and puts it in a project you pick. Both count as a thumbs-up.
  • Thumbs up and thumbs down say "more like this" and "less like this".
  • Dismiss hides a paper and counts as "not for me".

Rated and dismissed papers disappear from the list; tick Show rated to see them again. Papers you already have are marked In your library and sorted to the bottom. The strip at the top shows when the feed last fetched, how many papers it holds and how it is ranking right now. Refresh now fetches immediately (admins, or anybody on an instance with one user).

docs.title: How the ranking works
docs.text:
The method follows Scholar Inbox: Flicke et al., Scholar Inbox: Personalized Paper Recommendations for Scientists (arXiv 2504.08385). PaperManager has no connection to that service; this is a small local version of the same idea.

  1. Every new paper's title and abstract is turned into a list of numbers (an embedding) that places papers on similar topics close together.
  2. Your library teaches the feed what you like, and you do not have to rate anything for that. A real paper with an abstract or summary that you added yourself, or that sits in one of your projects, counts as a mild "yes" (a paper with neither embeds badly: fill missing abstracts). Ratings and bookmarks sharpen it: a paper you rated 4 or 5 stars, or bookmarked, is a clear "yes"; one you read and highlighted is a stronger "yes" than one that is merely kept; one you rated 1 or 2 stars is a "no". A paper counts once, by its strongest sign. Reference stubs (papers that only exist because another paper cites them) do not count. Your thumbs in the feed count too.
  3. From these "yes" and "no" papers, plus a random sample of the feed's other papers as a stand-in for "everything else", the server trains a small model (a logistic regression) that scores how likely you are to want a new paper.
  4. The list is sorted by that score.

Few signals at first. With fewer than 10 papers that count as a "yes" (added, in a project, rated, bookmarked, read or thumbs-up) there is not enough to train a model. The feed then sorts by how close each paper is to the nearest of those papers, and with none at all it shows the newest first. The strip tells you which of the three modes is active: Ranked by a model trained on N papers from your library, Ranked by similarity to N paper(s) from your library (a model needs 10), or Newest first.

Several people on one server. Ratings, bookmarks and reading status are stored once per paper, not per person. On an instance with several users they therefore only teach the feed about papers you added. What you added and what sits in projects you can see always counts as your own library, and so do your thumbs in the feed. On an instance with a single user all of them count.

How good is it? From 30 liked papers on, the strip shows a held-out AUC: the feed sets aside your newest likes, trains without them, and checks how often it ranks one of them above a random paper. 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect. It is a rough guide and not a promise.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: Everything stays on your instance: the fetched papers, your ratings, your choices and the model are stored in a small database in PAPER_FEED_DIR and never leave it. Embedding runs on your own server. The only requests that leave it go to arXiv and bioRxiv / medRxiv, and they carry nothing about you: the categories you chose, a date range and the User-Agent PaperManager-feed (plus the optional contact). Your library, your ratings and your name are never sent anywhere. (Add to library uses the normal URL ingest, which looks the paper up the same way pasting its link on the Library page does.)

docs.title: When something looks wrong
docs.text:
• The page says the feed is switched off. PAPER_FEED=true is missing on the server.
  • Nothing shows. Choose at least one category, then Refresh now. The first fetch takes a few minutes, because arXiv allows one request every three seconds.
  • arXiv answered "too many requests" or timed out. The feed waits as long as arXiv asks (30 to 120 s when it does not say), keeps to one request at a time and tries again. A category that did not finish is fetched again from the start at the next refresh; nothing is lost.
  • A problem is listed under the strip. One source failed on the last refresh (for example arXiv was unreachable). The other source still ran, and the next refresh tries again.
  • The ranking looks random. Rate a few papers. Ten papers that count as a "yes" switch the model on.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Similar papers: paste an abstract and look in the library and in the feed's candidates.
  • Switching the embedding model: what runs behind the ranking and how to change it.
  • Fill missing abstracts: papers without an abstract teach the feed less.

docs.title: Concepts, tour and concept map
docs.text:
Three tools help you understand papers rather than just store them. Concepts and the Tour work on one paper; the concept map works on a whole project.

Tool Where What you get Needs Concepts Paper view → Concepts tab Visual explanations of ideas, marked on the PDF page Claude (subscription or API key) Tour Paper view → Tour tab An overview and 6–12 stops through the PDF Claude Code on a subscription Concept map Projects → a project → Concept map One graph of the key concepts across all papers in the project An OpenAI-compatible model (LITELLM_*)

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
1. Open a paper with a PDF and switch to the Concepts tab.
  2. Click Find concepts. The pages are read in batches; on each page, up to three ideas that a picture explains best are marked.
  3. Click a concept to generate its visualisation, or Generate all for the rest.

Each concept gets one of four kinds of visualisation:

  • Formula: an equation broken into its parts, with what each symbol means
  • Graph: a plot drawn from data points (lines, points or bars)
  • Explanation: a short structured text
  • Animation: a small 2D animation, run in a sandboxed frame

Clicking a mark on the PDF opens its concept, and the other way round. This feature is adapted from Get It. (Apache-2.0).

docs.title: Quick tour
docs.text:
Open the Tour tab and click Make a quick tour. After a minute you get:

  • an overview of what the paper does and why it matters,
  • what to skip on a first read,
  • 6–12 stops, each tied to an exact passage in the PDF, with a short explanation and the concepts it relies on.

Click a stop, or press ← / →, and the PDF scrolls to that passage and highlights it. The tour is saved with the paper; Regenerate tour makes a new one.

Setup

The tour runs Sonnet through Claude Code on a Claude subscription. Set CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (from claude setup-token) and CLAUDE_CODE_USERS in .env. Without them the button stays disabled; there is no API-key fallback.

docs.title: Concept map
docs.text:
The concept map shows what a set of papers is about and how the ideas connect.

  • Circles are concepts; the colour is the kind (method, model, dataset, task, …) and the size is how many papers discuss it.
  • Papers can be shown too, sized by citations, with their authors optional.
  • Lines are typed relations from the papers: is a, part of, uses, extends, improves on, alternative to, evaluated on and more.
  • Filters narrow the map by author, year, kind and the minimum number of papers per concept. The list beside the graph groups all concepts by kind.

Papers are mapped automatically: every ten minutes, PaperManager maps project papers that have a summary but no concepts yet. Map new papers does it right away; Rebuild all starts over. Set CONCEPT_MAP_AUTO=false to switch the automatic run off.

For each paper the model returns 6–15 concepts with the paper's role for each (introduces, extends, uses, evaluates, critiques or background). It reuses names that already exist in the project, so the same idea from two papers becomes one circle.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text: A report is a long read written from your library: you ask a question (or pick a project), and PaperManager reads the relevant papers, their summaries, claims, your notes and highlights and passages of the full text, and writes a sectioned article that cites the papers it used. It runs in the background, so you can leave the page. Open Explore → Reports (/reports).

docs.title: Writing a report
docs.text:
In New report:

  1. Type a question, for example What do my papers say about guidance in diffusion models?
  2. Optionally pick a project to restrict the report to its papers. A project alone, with no question, gives an overview of that project's literature. Leave it on Whole library to search everything.
  3. Choose a length: Short (3 sections), Standard (5) or Long (7).
  4. Choose the model if more than one is offered (the default is the server's fast model; Claude on your own key writes better prose and costs more).
  5. Start it. The report appears in the list with a progress bar.

At most two reports are written at once on a server; the others wait as queued. Cancel (on the report page) stops one. A server restart marks a running report as failed; start it again.

docs.title: Reading a report
docs.text:
Click a report to open it. While it runs, the page shows the progress and the steps taken so far (scope, plan, evidence, sections, closing). The finished report has numbered sections, every claim followed by a citation marker that links to the paper, and a References list in order of first citation. A side panel lists the cited papers; a click opens the paper in your library.

Written by a model

Reports are AI-written from your papers. Check a claim against its source before you rely on it; the HTML export says so in a note with the model and the date.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
On the report page, Export Markdown and Export HTML; Delete removes the report:

  • Markdown: one .md file, citations as links to your library.
  • HTML: one self-contained page (styles inline, no external requests) that reads like an article, with the reference list linking to your library.

docs.title: Who sees a report
docs.text: Reports are private to the user who made them; admins can see and delete everyone's. Deleting a paper never deletes a report that cited it.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: Every step of a report is logged under the feature reports on the Tokens page. The pipeline is described in AI pipelines.

docs.title: Search and filters
docs.text: The Library search box and its Filters popover narrow the library by date added, year, status, properties and more. This page is the short version; Library has the full syntax, ranking weights and the list of sorts.

docs.title: Find what you added
docs.text:
1. Click Filters next to the search box (a bottom sheet on a phone). Every change applies at once, with or without a search query.
  2. Pick what you need, for example Added: Last 7 days and Properties: Has PDF: No to see what still needs a PDF.
  3. Active filters show as removable chips under the box, with Clear all.
Filter Options Added Any time, Today, Last 7, 30 or 90 days, or a custom range Year from and to year of publication Reading status Unread (including papers without a status), Reading, Read Rating at least 1 to 5 stars Document type Paper, Book, Lecture deck, News article Project papers in one project Properties Has PDF, Has full text, Has note, Has highlights, Bookmarked: each Any, Yes or No Tag, Topic, Venue start typing and pick from your own names Sort by relevance, newest or oldest added, recently updated, year, title, rating, citations

An author is picked in the search suggestions instead: type a name and choose the author.

docs.title: Everything is in the URL
docs.text: The query and all filters are kept in the address bar, so a view can be bookmarked or sent to a teammate with access to the same library: /?added=7d&has_pdf=0. Presets such as added=7d are relative to the moment the page opens. The parameter list is in Library.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: Browsing and filtering a large library is about two to three times faster than before: date, year and update time are indexed in the database, the paper count and the page are fetched in parallel, and a result is cached for 60 seconds, so paging or re-sorting the same search is served from memory. Any change you make (adding, editing, deleting) clears the cache. A server owner can turn the cache off with LIBRARY_SEARCH_CACHE=0. The API side is in the API reference.

docs.title: The Library landing page
docs.text: With no query and no filters the Library shows a header (Library · N papers), Continue reading (papers you marked Reading) and Recently added cards. The bar on top stays in view while you scroll: search box, Filters with a count badge, + to add papers, and a ⋯ menu with Surprise me, Find research gaps and the tag, topic, author and project managers.

docs.title: Similar papers
docs.text:
Explore → Similar papers (/similar) answers one question: does a paper like this already exist?

You write or paste an abstract, PaperManager compares its meaning with the abstracts of the papers in your library (and, if your instance runs the paper feed, with the new preprints it has fetched), and lists the closest ones with a similarity score. Use it to check whether a paper you are about to look for is already on your shelf, or whether something close has shown up in the feed.

The text can describe a paper that does not exist: "I am looking for work that trains a diffusion model on protein backbones with a fixed-length latent." The search does not need a real paper to start from.

Nothing leaves your instance. The text is embedded by the model that powers the library's semantic search (EMBED_MODEL, by default the small BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 on your own server's CPU); no outside service and no language-model API is called, so it costs no tokens.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Open Explore → Similar papers.
  2. Write or paste the text into the box. A title and one paragraph work best.
  3. Choose where to look (only if your instance has the feed): Library, Feed or Both.
  4. Optionally set Published since and the number of Results.
  5. Click Search.

Each result shows:

  • a similarity bar and the score (0 to 1, higher is closer);
  • a Library or Feed badge, and In your library on a feed paper you already have;
  • the title: a library paper opens its page in PaperManager, a feed paper opens on the preprint server;
  • authors, year or date, and a short abstract you can expand.

Two actions per result:

  • Add to library (feed papers you do not have yet) does the same as the Add button on the feed page.
  • Use this paper as the query copies its title and abstract into the box, without searching. Edit the text (cut a part away, add a sentence about what you want different) and search again. This is the quickest way to walk through a field: start from a paper you know, ask for its neighbours, pick the closest new one.

docs.title: What "scope" means
docs.text:
Scope Looks in Library the papers you may see: those outside every project and those in projects you are a member of Feed the feed's candidates, the preprints it has fetched and kept (30 days by default, longer if somebody rated them; see Paper feed) Both both lists merged by score

Without the feed the toggle is not shown and the search runs on the library. Reference stubs (papers that only exist because another paper cites them, tagged from-references) are left out, because a title alone embeds poorly.

Published since limits feed papers by their publication date. A library paper only has a year, so it is compared by year alone: with 1 October 2026 a library paper from 2026 stays in, one from 2025 goes; library papers without a year are left out when you set a date.

docs.title: Writing a good query
docs.text:
• Write an abstract, not keywords. The index holds title and abstract text, and a text of the same shape lands near it. A bare "diffusion protein" is treated as a short search phrase and matches loosely.
  • Say what the work does and how, in the words a paper would use: the problem, the method, the result.
  • Hypothetical is fine. Describe the paper you wish existed. A high score on a result means that paper probably exists; if the best score is low, probably nobody has written it, or the library does not hold it.
  • Keep to a title and a paragraph. Only roughly the first 200 words are used (the same limit as the stored papers), so a long text is read from its start.
  • Vary it. Two or three wordings of the same idea show you whether the neighbours are stable.

As a rough guide for the default model (scores of another model sit on another scale), a score above about 0.8 is a close match, 0.6 to 0.8 related work, and below 0.6 weak.

docs.title: Using it from Claude (MCP)
docs.text:
If you have connected Claude to your library, two tools do the same search:

  • find_similar_papers(text, scope="both", k=10, since="", min_score=0.0)
  • papers_like(paper_id, scope="both", k=10)

Give find_similar_papers a title and a paragraph, not keywords. Example prompt:

Here is the abstract of a paper I wish existed: "Sparse attention for long documents ... (a paragraph)". Check with find_similar_papers whether something like it is already in my library or in the feed since 1 October, and tell me which results are really the same idea and which only share the topic.

The tools return titles, links, scores, whether a feed paper is already in your library, and a 300-character snippet. The MCP server reads the same index as the app, so it needs the same VECTOR_STORE_DIR (and, for the feed, PAPER_FEED and PAPER_FEED_DIR) as the backend, and a running backend to embed your text.

docs.title: When it says the index is not ready
docs.text:
The page shows The index is not ready for this search with the reason, and the same text appears as available: false from the API and the tools. It happens when

  • the server has just started and is still building the index of the library (a few minutes for a large library; the first start after switching on semantic search takes longest),
  • the embedding model was changed (EMBED_MODEL) and the index is being rebuilt with it, or a prepared one has not been adopted yet (it answers again as soon as a complete index for the new model is in place; see Switching the embedding model),
  • the embedding model is still loading after a start,
  • semantic search is switched off (LIBRARY_SEMANTIC=false), or
  • you chose Feed and the feed has not embedded any papers yet.

Try again in a few minutes. With Both, one list that is not ready is named in a note and the other still answers.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Quality depends on the embedding model and on the abstracts you hold. The default model is small and fast; it finds topics and approaches well and subtle differences poorly. The operator can choose a larger or scientific model. A paper in your library without an abstract (or with only a title) embeds badly and will rarely be found: fill the missing abstracts of papers that have a DOI. If the library has a summary instead of an abstract, the summary is used.
  • Similar is not the same. A high score says two texts are about the same thing, not that one paper repeats the other. Read the abstract before deciding.
  • Feed papers are only recent ones from the sources and categories your instance chose; the feed is a window, not an archive.
  • Other users' papers stay hidden. You only get papers you may see, and on a shared instance a feed paper is marked In your library only if it is among them. Your thumbs-ups and thumbs-downs from the feed are yours alone.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Paper feed: the new preprints that the Feed scope searches.
  • Fill missing abstracts: gives papers without an abstract something to be found by.
  • Switching the embedding model: changes what "similar" means.

docs.title: Suggestions
docs.text: Explore → Suggestions (/suggestions) is where improvements to PaperManager are collected: ideas the knowledge chat proposes, ideas you write yourself, and everyone's votes on them.

docs.title: Where suggestions come from
docs.text:
• From the chat. When a conversation shows that PaperManager lacks something you needed, the answer can end with a small chip with one concrete idea. The chip links here, has a vote button, and × hides it. If the same idea is already open or planned, the chat adds your vote and counts the repeat (seen 3x) instead of making a duplicate.
  • By hand. Use Suggest an improvement: a short title (3 to 280 characters) and, optionally, what you were trying to do and what got in the way.

docs.title: Voting and status
docs.text:
Click the vote button to back a suggestion, click again to take the vote back. The tabs filter by status: Open, Planned, Done, Dismissed or All; sort by most votes or newest. Only admins change the status. The author or an admin can edit the text or delete a suggestion.

Suggestions are shared by everyone on the instance, because they are about the app and not about your papers. A server owner can turn off recording of chat suggestions with SUGGESTIONS_FROM_CHAT=false.

docs.title: Switching the embedding model
docs.text:
PaperManager turns every paper's title and abstract into a vector (an embedding). Library search, the paper feed and similar papers all compare those vectors. The default model is small (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, 384 numbers per paper) and runs on the backend's CPU. A larger model, for example a scientific one such as J0nasW/sciembed-full (ModernBERT-base, 768 numbers, MIT licence), can place related papers closer together (which one to choose).

For the operator of the server. This page is not about using the app but about changing what it runs on.

docs.title: Choosing an embedding model
docs.text:
The stock default, BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (384 numbers per paper, about 130 MB, fast on a CPU), is a good general-purpose choice and nothing has to be done to use it. Switching is optional.

A model trained on scientific text can place related papers closer together. One example is J0nasW/sciembed-full (ModernBERT-base fine-tuned on citation contexts of scientific papers, 768 numbers per paper, MIT licence). Of 13 models compared on one real library it was the best for citation-neighbour recall (how many of a paper's cited and citing papers appear among its ten nearest neighbours), but by a small margin over the default.

Any model can be measured the same way with backend/scripts/embedder_benchmark.py, which scores models on an export of your own library (citation-neighbour recall, topic agreement, the feed's held-out AUC, speed). How to run it and how to read the numbers is in the embedding benchmark.

Treat any published ranking with care, including this one: results on one library do not transfer automatically to another. A different field, language, mix of abstracts and titles or library size can change the order. If the difference matters to you, run the benchmark on your own library before you re-embed everything. A model that is only a little better on paper is rarely worth hours of work.

docs.title: Why this needs a procedure
docs.text:
Vectors of two models cannot be compared, so a switch means embedding the whole library again: one text per paper, plus the feed's stored candidates and the feed's cache of library vectors. If you only change EMBED_MODEL and restart, the backend does exactly that on its own CPU, in the background. For a library of about ten thousand papers and a base-sized model that takes hours, and search answers by keywords meanwhile.

The tools described here move that bulk job to any machine with a CUDA GPU (a few minutes) and leave the everyday work, embedding the handful of papers that arrive each day, with the backend's CPU and the same model. The new vectors are prepared next to the live ones, the backend adopts them when it restarts with the new setting, and the old ones are kept so that you can go back.

docs.title: The five steps
docs.text:
All commands start in the backend's environment (below: the Docker Compose service named backend, which is app in docker-compose.selfhost.yml, and the persistent volume mounted at /data, which is /app/data there; use python scripts/... directly from the backend/ folder if you run it without Docker). The export folder holds the text of your whole library, so it must not live in a git checkout. vectors_export.py refuses such a path.

1. Export the texts (in the backend environment):

docker compose exec backend python scripts/vectors_export.py \
    --out /data/vector_export --model J0nasW/sciembed-full
docker compose cp backend:/data/vector_export ~/vector_export

This reads the library (and, when PAPER_FEED=true, the feed's candidates) and writes spec.json (model, dimension, pooling, prefixes, text format, 256-token limit, counts) and one <namespace>.jsonl file per vector set: library, feed, feed_library. A model that PaperManager does not list needs --dim N (and --pooling cls|mean, --doc-prefix ...) as well. Nothing is written to the databases.

The export is made with direct database access and no per-user filtering, like the sync thread that builds the search index: the vector index is shared by every user of the instance and only the final result lists are filtered by who may see what. Delete the folder when you are done.

2. Copy it to a GPU machine:

scp -r ~/vector_export user@gpu-host:~/
scp backend/scripts/embed_bulk.py user@gpu-host:~/

3. Embed there. embed_bulk.py is one file that needs only torch (with CUDA), transformers (4.48 or newer for ModernBERT models) and numpy; no PaperManager code, no database, no key:

python embed_bulk.py ~/vector_export --device cuda

It embeds in float16 with a batch size that halves when the GPU runs out of memory, prints progress, and writes <namespace>.npy (float32, unit length) and <namespace>.ids.json next to the export. Run again after an interruption: finished namespaces are skipped. --offline --model /path/to/model uses a local copy of the model; --device cpu works too, only slowly. It truncates at 256 tokens, pools and normalises exactly like the backend's CPU embedder (a test keeps the two equal), so the vectors the backend makes later for new papers sit in the same space.

4. Copy the results back and import them:

scp user@gpu-host:~/vector_export/*.npy user@gpu-host:~/vector_export/*.json ~/vector_export/
docker compose cp ~/vector_export backend:/data/
docker compose exec backend python scripts/vectors_import.py /data/vector_export

The import checks each namespace (dimension, one vector per id, no NaN, unit length, the vectors belong to the exported texts) and then re-embeds 20 random texts on the backend's CPU with the real embedder, requiring a mean cosine of at least 0.98 to the imported vectors (float16 on the GPU against float32 here). It needs the model on the backend; if it cannot load it, it says so and imports unverified; --skip-check skips the check on purpose. The vectors are stored as a prepared generation: not live, no lock on the running backend, nothing about the current index changes and search keeps working. It prints the ids the live index holds that the import lacks (papers added since the export), which the normal sync embeds later. vectors_import.py DIR --discard throws a prepared generation away; importing again replaces it.

5. Switch. Set the model in the backend's environment (.env) and restart:

EMBED_MODEL=J0nasW/sciembed-full
CONFERENCE_EMBED_MODEL=BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5

J0nasW/sciembed-full is in the built-in list (768 dimensions, mean pooling, no prefixes). For another model add EMBED_DIM, EMBED_POOLING and the prefixes the import printed. On start the backend finds the prepared generation for exactly this setting, adopts it instead of re-embedding, and the sync embeds only papers that are missing or whose text changed since the export. The old generation stays on disk as the rollback target.

CONFERENCE_EMBED_MODEL is optional but recommended: the conference explorer keeps its own saved vectors, built with the old model. It reads CONFERENCE_EMBED_MODEL first and EMBED_MODEL only when that is empty, so setting it to the old model keeps the explorer's topic search working while the library moves on. Both models are then loaded in the backend (about 130 MB and 600 MB). Without it the explorer follows EMBED_MODEL, its vectors no longer fit, and its topic search falls back to keywords until its datasets are rebuilt.

docs.title: Going back
docs.text:
The generation a model switch replaces is kept: VECTOR_STORE_KEEP_GENERATIONS (default 2) counts the live generation, so one older one is kept per vector set (3 keeps two, 1 keeps none). Two ways back:

  • Set EMBED_MODEL (and the other settings) back to the old values and restart. The backend finds the kept generation of that setting and adopts it instead of rebuilding; papers added since are embedded by the sync.
  • Or stop the backend and run python scripts/vectors_rollback.py (--status lists what is live, kept and prepared). It swaps the kept generations back and prints the exact settings to put back into .env. The environment variables must then be set back before the restart: with the new model still configured the backend would see the restored generation as outdated and adopt the other one again. A rollback can be undone by running the script again.

docs.title: What happens to search and the feed
docs.text:
• Search is never mixed. Each vector set records the model it was built with. While it does not match the configured model (for instance after an EMBED_MODEL change that nothing was prepared for), library search and similar papers answer by keywords and the feed sees no vectors, until a matching generation is adopted or the rebuild has finished. A query is always embedded with the model of the vectors it is compared with.
  • The feed retrains by itself. Its classifier is fitted from vectors in memory and is not stored: after the switch the next ranking uses the new vectors. Candidates and cached library vectors that arrived after the export are embedded in the next refresh; candidates purged since the export are dropped from the adopted set.
  • Rebuilds still work. A start with a new EMBED_MODEL and no prepared generation behaves as before: a new generation is built in the background on the CPU and swapped in when complete (the old one is kept for a rollback there as well).
  • Disk. A kept generation costs papers x dimension x 4 bytes plus a small database: about 17 MB for ten thousand papers at 384 dimensions, 31 MB at 768.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Variable Default Meaning EMBED_MODEL BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 Model of library search, the feed and similar papers EMBED_DIM, EMBED_POOLING, EMBED_QUERY_PREFIX, EMBED_DOC_PREFIX from the model Only for a model that is not in the built-in list, or to override it CONFERENCE_EMBED_MODEL empty The explorer's model; read first, EMBED_MODEL only when empty. A model other than EMBED_MODEL takes CONFERENCE_EMBED_DIM, _POOLING, _QUERY_PREFIX, _DOC_PREFIX when it is not in the built-in list VECTOR_STORE_KEEP_GENERATIONS 2 Generations kept per vector set after a model switch, the live one included

Models are loaded without trust_remote_code: a model that needs custom code from its repository is not supported here. Developer notes are in .specs/019_vector_store.md.

docs.text:
• Paper feed and similar papers: the two features whose ranking changes with the model.
  • Fill missing abstracts: the vectors are built from title and abstract, so do this first if many papers lack one.
  • Conference explorer: keeps its own vectors, see CONFERENCE_EMBED_MODEL above.

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text: Account menu → Tokens (/tokens) shows what the language models behind PaperManager are used for and what that costs at list price. Every model call the app makes is written to a ledger: summaries, topic suggestions, claims, chat answers, concept cards, tours, researcher CVs, reports.

docs.title: What the page shows
docs.text:
Pick a time range (7, 30 or 90 days); admins can also narrow by user, feature or model.

  • Totals: spend in the range, spend today, number of calls, input and output tokens (with how many were read from the prompt cache) and errors.
  • Cost per day (per week for long ranges), as a bar chart.
  • By feature, by model and, for admins, by user: calls, tokens and cost, most expensive first. A model that is not in the price table is flagged, and its calls count without a price.
  • Most expensive calls and most expensive papers: where a bulk import or a long report went.
  • Recent calls: the newest calls one by one, with feature, model, tokens, cost, latency and any error.
  • Prices: the USD-per-million-token table the costs are computed from, and the date it was last updated.

Each user sees their own calls. Admins see everyone's.

docs.title: How costs are counted
docs.text:
• Anthropic and OpenAI calls are priced from the table, including cached-input discounts.
  • Models on the self-hosted LiteLLM proxy cost 0 (your own hardware).
  • Claude Code on a subscription is not billed per token; its list-price equivalent is shown separately and left out of the billed total.
  • Streamed answers are recorded when they finish. If a provider reports no usage for a stream, the tokens are estimated from the text length and marked as estimated.

The ledger is a SQLite file kept next to the app's data, so it survives rebuilds and does not add nodes to your graph. Recording can be switched off with USAGE_LEDGER_ENABLED=false; extra or changed prices go in a JSON file named by USAGE_PRICES_FILE. See Architecture.

The Health page shows today's spend from the same ledger.

docs.title: Topic map
docs.text: Explore → Topic map (/topic-map) shows your whole library as one map: every paper with an embedding is a dot, and papers that are about similar things sit close together. The map fills the page; the settings are on the right (on a phone, tap Settings for a bottom sheet). Every setting is kept in the address, so you can link a view or reload it.

docs.title: Reading the map
docs.text:
• Big dots are your library papers; small faint dots are references (cited papers without a PDF).
  • Hover a dot for its title, topic and year; click to open the paper.
  • Drag to pan, Ctrl/⌘ + scroll (or pinch) to zoom, or use + / −; Reset zoom appears once you zoom in.
  • The legend under the map matches the colour setting.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting What it does Colour by Cluster (default), Project, Year (light to dark scale), Reading status, or None References Show or hide the cited papers (library papers only / both) Cluster labels, label size Turn the labels on or off and change their size Dot size, dot opacity Sliders Number of clusters 4 to 16 (default: automatic). The first time you pick a number the map is re-clustered in the background ("Re-clustering…"), and the result is remembered Projects Check one or more projects: each gets a soft bubble in its colour, the rest fades Year from / to Hide papers outside the range Highlight titles containing Dims every paper whose title does not contain all the words Reset Back to the defaults

Labels never reveal papers you cannot see: for non-admin users they are derived from papers that are in no project.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
Export PNG downloads topic-map-YYYY-MM-DD.png at 2× (PNG 4× for print): the current view with your settings, zoom and highlights, the legend and a title, on a white background. Copy image puts the same picture on the clipboard (browsers that allow it, on https or localhost).

The Library page's map card has an Open full map ↗ link.
